expectations.text: Identifies functional layers for chat: message input, message delivery/routing, message display, history/persistence, presence/status
expectations.evidence: Output identifies 6 layers covering all required dimensions: Layer 1 (Customer initiates contact = message input), Layer 2 (Route to agent = delivery/routing), Layer 3 (Message exchange = input/display), Layer 4 (Conversation persistence = history/persistence), Layer 5 (Agent availability/status = presence/status), Layer 6 (Conversation resolution). All specified layer types are represented.

expectations.text: Generates at least 4 options per layer with quality gradient
expectations.evidence: Every layer has exactly 5 options (e.g. 1.1–1.5, 2.1–2.5) with a clear manual-to-enterprise gradient. Example: Layer 3 goes from '3.1 Exchange happens via email replies — no real-time component' up to '3.5 WebSocket with presence indicators, typing indicators, read receipts, file attachments'.

expectations.text: The smallest vertical slice does NOT use WebSockets, Kafka, or Redis — uses polling, email, or manual checking instead
expectations.evidence: Slice 1 picks options 1.2 (static HTML form emailed to inbox), 2.1 (one agent, no routing), 3.1 (email thread back-and-forth), 4.1 (email IS the persistence), 5.1 (agent checks inbox), 6.2 (agent archives email). Step 3 explicitly states: 'This slice requires zero new infrastructure. No WebSockets, no Redis, no Kafka, no new database tables.'

expectations.text: Explicitly challenges whether 'real-time' is needed for the first slice — asks 'can we validate the core value without real-time infrastructure?'
expectations.evidence: Step 4 explicitly eliminates 'Everything requiring WebSocket infrastructure (3.4, 3.5) — too slow to set up'. Step 5 frames the decision as: 'Decision it answers: "Can customers reach a human and get a response?" — validated before investing in any chat infrastructure.' The self-check also flags '[x] No new infrastructure required in Slice 1 (no WebSockets, no Redis, no message broker)'. The challenge is implicit rather than posed as an explicit question, but the substance is present and clear.

expectations.text: Includes at least one 'manual/crutch' option per layer — e.g., support agent checks an email inbox instead of a realtime dashboard
expectations.evidence: Every layer has at least one manual/crutch option: Layer 1 — '1.1 Customer sends an email to support@company.com — agent replies manually'; Layer 2 — '2.1 All chats go to one person (the only agent) — no routing needed'; Layer 3 — '3.1 Exchange happens via email replies — no real-time component'; Layer 4 — '4.1 No persistence — conversation exists only in email thread or browser session'; Layer 5 — '5.1 No status — agents just check the inbox when they feel like it'; Layer 6 — '6.1 No formal close — conversation just goes cold'.

expectations.text: The smallest slice is designed to validate the core user value (customer gets help) before investing in real-time infrastructure
expectations.evidence: Step 5 directly states: 'Who gets value: Any customer who needs help gets a response. The support agent has a single, familiar inbox to work from.' and 'Decision it answers: "Can customers reach a human and get a response?" — validated before investing in any chat infrastructure.' The slice is explicitly framed as a value-validation checkpoint.

claims.claim: This slice requires zero new infrastructure — no WebSockets, no Redis, no Kafka, no new database tables
claims.evidence: All options chosen for Slice 1 are email-based (1.2, 3.1) or require no technology at all (2.1, 4.1, 5.1, 6.2). The claim is fully consistent with the selected layer options.

claims.claim: Build time is 2–4 hours for Slice 1
claims.evidence: Slice 1 is an HTML form + one email-send endpoint + env var for inbox address. The estimate is plausible and consistent with the minimal technical scope.

claims.claim: 4-5 options per layer following quality gradient
claims.evidence: All 6 layers have exactly 5 options each, confirmed by counting in the output (1.1–1.5, 2.1–2.5, 3.1–3.5, 4.1–4.5, 5.1–5.5, 6.1–6.5).

claims.claim: Slice 2 uses a free-tier hosted widget (Tawk.to, Crisp) with no backend code for transport
claims.evidence: Step 6 Slice 2 explicitly describes upgrading to a SaaS chat widget, noting 'No backend code required for the transport layer' and lists Tawk.to/Crisp as examples — consistent with layer option 1.3.

suggestions.assertion: Explicitly challenges whether 'real-time' is needed for the first slice — asks 'can we validate the core value without real-time infrastructure?'
suggestions.reason: The assertion requires an 'explicit challenge' phrased as a question. The output satisfies the spirit — it eliminates real-time options with clear reasoning and frames Slice 1 as a value-validation step — but never poses the challenge as a direct rhetorical question to the reader. A tighter assertion would specify 'the output must include a sentence that questions whether real-time is necessary for the first slice', making it easier to distinguish genuine pushback from a model that just happened to pick low-tech options.

No assertion checks whether message *display* is a distinct layer. The expectation list names it, but the output merges message input and display into a single 'Message exchange' layer. A discriminating assertion would verify they are treated as separate layers (or explicitly accept merging them) so this design decision is visible to the evaluator.

No assertion verifies that the follow-up slices (Slice 2, 3, 4) progressively introduce infrastructure rather than jumping to full real-time in one step. A skill that outputs an excellent Slice 1 but proposes WebSockets+Kafka+Redis all in Slice 2 would pass all current assertions. Adding a check for incremental infrastructure graduation would make the eval more discriminating.

eval_feedback.overall: Evals are well-targeted and the output satisfies all of them with clear evidence. The main gap is the lack of an assertion on incremental infrastructure in follow-up slices, and the 'explicit challenge' assertion could be tightened to require a specific sentence rather than accepting implied pushback.
